arguments.value:
The agreement lets STW explore, drill, deepen, and operate water wells in the City of Fort Stockton’s Capitan Reef Aquifer property at STW’s expense, with access to the land and use of needed surface areas for pumping and filling stations. STW must restore any damage, carry insurance, and follow applicable laws and regulations. The deal lasts 30 years and renews yearly unless properly terminated.

STW must first deepen the existing well or, if that fails, drill a replacement well, then pay for hydrogeological studies to determine water quantity and quality. If the studies show the wells can produce at least 1,200 gallons per minute and the water meets required standards, STW may exercise an option to produce and transport water, pay the City a $5 million bonus, and then owe a 17% royalty on water sold from the property. The City also gets up to 3 million gallons per day for its own use at no cost when it requests delivery.

If the wells do not meet the target, STW may walk away, continue anyway without reimbursement, or proceed under the agreement if regulators approve a lower amount. STW can also drill additional wells if needed for new contracts. STW owns the wells during the agreement, but title reverts to the City if the property-related rights end and the City reimburses STW as required.

The City must provide documents and cooperate with studies and approvals, and STW is responsible for obtaining regulatory approvals. STW may use certain City easements and infrastructure for other Pecos County water projects and pay a 7% royalty on water sold from those other properties. The agreement also includes termination rights, reimbursement rules, indemnity, notice requirements, governing law in Texas, and other standard contract terms.
